To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Cu and Zn isotope ratios in wild-type mouse brain are constant, but that the Cu isotope ratios in the brain of mice expressing PrP lacking the metal binding domain are significantly enriched in 65Cu.
the Cu and Zn isotoe ratios are not affected by knockout or overexpression of PrPC, but are altered when PrPC is lacking the copper binding domain.
the expression of PrP can alter the Cu isotope ratio in the brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the partitioning of Cu and the Zn isotopes in biological systems.
the role of proteins in the partitioning of metals in biological systems.
understanding how metal isotopes partition in biological systems and how they can be used as tracers to study the function of proteins and pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PrP is a key protein for Cu and Zn isotoe distribution in the brain and the isotope ratio of these elements can be used as a biomarker for the expression of the PrP.
the Cu isotope ratio in brain is not altered by the absence of PrP, but is increased by the overexpression of PrPC.
the isotope ratios are not significantly different between the different mouse strains and that the PrP expression can influence the isotope ratios in a biological system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the isotope ratio of Cu and Zn in the mouse brain is not altered significantly by genetic manipulation of the prion gene.
Cu and Zn is a complex process in the brain and the prion protein is one of the factors involved in this process.
the prion protein may be involved in the partitioning of Cu isotopes, but not Zn isotopes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the isotope ratios for these elements are not fixed, and the ratios in a biological context can vary.
the isotope ratios of Cu and Zn in mouse brain can be altered by the expression of a copper binding protein.
metal isotope ratios can be altered by the expression of proteins.
